title: Is Insurance a Bad Bet?
objective: After this level you can explain why insurance loses money on average for buyers yet can still be a sensible choice.
summary: Insurance premiums must cover claims, running costs and profit, so buyers lose a little on average. Risk-averse people pay that extra to swap a big possible loss for a small sure cost.

cards.headline: Insurance companies make money. So, on average, their customers lose it.
cards.body: As a bet, insurance loses. Yet buying it can still be a smart move. Expected value is part of the story, but not all of it.

cards.headline: A pool that pays out less than it takes in
cards.body: Insurance is a pool. Members pay a regular premium, and anyone who suffers a covered loss is paid from the pool. Over time, the premiums have to cover three things: the claims, the cost of running the company, and its profit. So the average customer pays in more than they get back. For the buyer, insurance has a negative expected value.

cards.headline: The $1,000 bike
cards.body: Say your bike is worth $1,000, and each year there's a 1 in 100 chance you'll have to replace it. Your expected loss is $1,000 × 1/100, or $10 a year. An insurer would charge that $10 plus a little extra, and the extra is how it makes money. Most years you pay and get nothing back. That's the deal working, not failing.

cards.fact: You pay a little extra to swap a big gamble for a small, sure cost.
cards.context: Economists call people risk-averse when they'll pay more than a gamble's expected loss to avoid it, and most people are. Insurance exists so that no single event hits you too hard. So the question isn't only "is the average in my favor?" It's also "what happens to me if the bad outcome comes?"

options.label: There is no average; it is pure luck
options.rationale: Individual years are luck, but the average is set by the premiums.
